title: I give in, you guys are right (about coding)
author: freknil
selftext:
The models since September have really changed everything. I'm using ChatGPTs Luna 6 (the free tier) and i'm basically able to make prototypes without any real limitations. I'm able to use all the softskills I've gained from human programming to break down prompts into small actionable tasks. From that point on i've been able to achieve the goal of each prompt within 1 prompt (90% of the time) or within a 2nd prompt (10% of the time). And most of the 2nd prompts are because I left out a specific design detail that a human could have easily overlooked.

I just do very small actionable steps to get there with context about why it is done. Exactly like I would do when writing a Jira ticket for an engineer that lacks context of the customers experience.

The code structure can be fucking atrocious and i've often felt like i've had to specifically explain how I want it structured so I can do design work but like... that's it. That's my only real complaint. Programming as a hard skill is basically over, programming as a soft skill is still valuable. 

So many people i know in the past month have transitioned over to AI and they all say the same thing... "there is no going back". The only real advantage human coded games have now a days is marketing because gamers can quickly associating it with higher default levels of quality. But like with games made with premade assets or games made with unity, that stigma is going to dissolve as genuinely good AI coded games get created and gamers are forced to take on a more nuanced takes to avoid low effort garbage.

I'm going to keep my human crafted games, human crafted. It's really helps me with marketing since the stigma around AI is still potent. But I can already see it dissolving. You see more and more AI games succeed to the point where I can't really call them exceptions anymore. A couple of big AI games coming out will completely changing the narrative in 2027, and by 2028 it will just be normal and what will differentiate good games from bad games will be the same thing that has always differentiated them. Iteration.

It kind of sucks having a large part of my skill set be made obsolete, but the soft skills transfer over extremely easily and I think that as a whole, I will be able to make significantly better games because of AI.

replies.author: AmbroSnoopi
replies.body:
Pls don’t waste your time and tokens on Fable. 

I’d recommend you try Opus on Medium. It’s more than enough for the approach you described (well-defined, story-sized requests). The only benefit you are likely to experience is, that it gives you better code quality than “older” models (though with good direction it’s barely noticeable).

Then you can experiment with omitting more and more context and marvel at how it figures it all out nonetheless.

Finally, you can dare cranking it up to High or Extra and giving it a feature-sized prompt. Most of the times, it will do a really good job, often with beautiful expert level architecture. The catch is “most of the times”…  
I’m scared of letting slop creep in, so I still review evey line of code. And let me tell you: trying to spot export-looking slop in mostly expert-level PRs is a real headache.

TL;DR: keep your discipline and move in small steps. You’ll go farther, and possibly still faster.

i think everyone is right, the frontier models the past few months really have changed everything, it's impossible to deny the benefits now. even if you prefer to have more control, it is still unbelievably good at tracing logic and running automatic behavior. it's impossible to imagine going back to working without it.
